title: .NET collections and their cost
sub: What is inside List, Queue, Dictionary, PriorityQueue, SortedSet and LinkedList, what each operation costs, and what Unity lacks
cards/0/title: The cost of an operation is part of the solution
cards/0/body:
The complexity of a solution is the number of operations times the cost of each. The same algorithm with a different collection has a different complexity. Removing duplicates while keeping the order: with List<T>.Contains every check is a linear scan, O(n), and the whole solution is O(n²); with HashSet<T> a check is O(1) on average, and the solution is O(n). For n = 10⁵ that is 5·10⁹ operations versus 10⁵.

That is why interviewers ask about every collection you use: “why this one, and what does the operation cost”. The answer is not “it is fast” but a bound and the structure: “HashSet is a hash table, Add and Contains are O(1) on average”. This lesson is the price list of .NET collections and which of them Unity has.
cards/1/title: List<T>: an array and a counter
cards/1/body:
List<T> is an array plus a Count. Every price follows from that.

O(1): the indexer list[i], Add (amortized — from the previous lesson), RemoveAt(Count − 1) — removing the last element.
O(n): Insert(i, x) and RemoveAt(i) at the front or in the middle — every element to the right is shifted with Array.Copy; Contains, IndexOf, Remove(x) — a linear scan.
O(n log n): Sort; once sorted, BinarySearch is O(log n).

A trick worth knowing: when order does not matter, an element in the middle is removed in O(1) — move the last element into its place and remove the last. In a game this is how you clean up a list of live enemies or bullets: their order means nothing.
cards/2/body:
Stack<T> is an array whose end is the top: Push (amortized), Pop and Peek are O(1). The order is “last in, first out” (LIFO): depth-first search, brackets, undo.

Queue<T> is a circular buffer over an array: two indices, head (where you take from) and tail (where you put to), and each wraps to the start when it reaches the end of the array. So Enqueue (amortized) and Dequeue are O(1), and nothing is ever shifted. When the buffer is full, the queue doubles the array and copies the elements over in order. The order is “first in, first out” (FIFO): breadth-first search, event queues.

Neither gives access by index (LINQ ElementAt is a linear scan here), and neither shrinks on its own. There are TryPop and TryDequeue — no exception on an empty collection.
cards/3/q: A job queue is built on a List<int>: Add at the end, RemoveAt(0) from the front. Up to 10⁵ jobs sit in it at once, and all of them pass through it. What is wrong?
cards/3/options/0: RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list: O(n) per removal, on the order of 10⁹–10¹⁰ shifts in total. You need a Queue<T>
cards/3/options/1: Nothing: List<T> is an array, and removing from it is O(1)
cards/3/options/2: Add becomes O(n) because the list keeps growing
cards/3/options/3: The only problem is memory: List<T> does not release space after RemoveAt
cards/3/explain: Removing from the front of an array shifts every element to its right by one slot. 10⁵ removals, each shifting tens of thousands of elements, is billions of operations. Queue<T> is a circular buffer: Dequeue just moves head, O(1).
cards/3/wrong/1: Only removing the last element is O(1). RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole tail with Array.Copy.
cards/3/wrong/2: Add stays amortized O(1): the capacity doubles. It is removal from the front that is expensive.
cards/3/wrong/3: The capacity indeed does not shrink, but that is minor. The real trouble is O(n) for every RemoveAt(0).
cards/4/title: Dictionary and HashSet: O(1) on average
cards/4/body:
A hash table: key → GetHashCode() → bucket number; the bucket holds a short chain of entries compared with Equals. If the hashes are spread evenly, a bucket holds one or two entries, and TryGetValue, ContainsKey, Add, Remove are O(1) on average. The average here is over the keys: if the keys land in one bucket (a bad GetHashCode or deliberately crafted data), a lookup turns into a walk along the chain — O(n) in the worst case.

When the entry array is full (as many entries as buckets), the table grows to roughly twice the size (a prime) and redistributes every entry — O(n), but rarely: insertion is amortized O(1). If n is known, pass the capacity to the constructor.

Habits: TryGetValue is one lookup instead of the two of ContainsKey + indexer; the indexer d[k] = v overwrites, while Add throws on a duplicate key; HashSet.Add returns false if the element was already there. The enumeration order is not guaranteed — do not rely on it.
cards/5/body:
A heap (binary) is a tree laid out in an array with no pointers: element i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the invariant is that a parent is no greater than its children. So the minimum is always at the root, a[0]. Insert: put the element at the end and move it up, swapping with the parent while the parent is greater. Remove the minimum: put the last element in place of the root and move it down towards the smaller child. The tree height is log n, so both operations are O(log n), and looking at the minimum is O(1). Do not confuse it with the managed heap where objects live: it is one word for two different things.

.NET 6+ has one ready-made — PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>: a min-heap by priority, Enqueue and Dequeue are O(log n), Peek is O(1). Inside it is a 4-ary heap: each node has four children, so the tree is shallower. What it lacks:

1. Changing a priority (decrease-key). The workaround is lazy deletion: enqueue the element again with the new priority and skip the stale copy when it comes out.
2. Order among equals: elements with the same priority come out in arbitrary order — the queue is not stable. If you need an order, add the insertion number to the priority.
3. Search: there is no Contains, and Remove only arrived in .NET 9 and costs O(n).

A max-heap is made with a reversed comparer. In Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) there is no PriorityQueue: you write your own binary heap over an array or use a SortedSet — more on it below.
cards/5/deep:
The 4-ary heap. Node i has its parent at (i − 1) / 4 and children at 4i + 1 … 4i + 4. There are log₄ n levels — half as many as in a binary heap — so moving up during Enqueue is shorter. Moving down during Dequeue compares up to four children per level, but they sit next to each other in memory — fewer cache misses. The asymptotics are the same, O(log n).

Building in O(n). The constructor from a collection and EnqueueRange into an empty queue do not insert one by one (O(n log n)); they build the heap bottom-up in O(n): most nodes are near the bottom and do not have far to sink. EnqueueDequeue (.NET 6) pushes and pops the minimum in a single sift — handy for “the best k”: keep a min-heap of k elements, and the worst of the best is always at the root.

Enumeration. UnorderedItems yields the elements in array order, not by priority. Sorted output only comes from successive Dequeue calls, O(n log n).

Your own heap in Unity. A binary heap over T[] with manual growth is about 40 lines and allocates nothing after warm-up. SortedSet<(int priority, int id)> is shorter to write and supports decrease-key (remove and insert again), but every Add is a new tree node on the heap, that is, garbage for the GC.
cards/6/q: What is true about PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>? Select all.
cards/6/options/0: Peek is O(1), Dequeue is O(log n)
cards/6/options/1: Unity has it out of the box since 2021.2
cards/6/options/2: You cannot change the priority of an element in the queue: you enqueue a copy and skip the stale one
cards/6/options/3: Elements with equal priority come out in insertion order
cards/6/options/4: To get the maximum out, you pass a reversed comparer
cards/6/explain: The minimum sits at the root — Peek is O(1), and Dequeue sinks the new root through the height of the tree — O(log n). There is no decrease-key, hence lazy deletion. A max-heap is a Comparer with b.CompareTo(a). Unity does not have the class: it arrived in .NET 6, and Unity is .NET Standard 2.1. Equal priorities come out in arbitrary order: a heap is not stable.
cards/7/body:
SortedSet<T> is a red-black tree: a binary search tree (smaller to the left, larger to the right) that recolours and rotates nodes on inserts and deletes so that the height stays at most 2·log₂(n + 1). So Add, Remove, Contains are O(log n) in the worst case, not just on average. Min and Max are O(log n): a walk down to the outermost node. Enumeration goes in ascending order. GetViewBetween(lo, hi) returns the range [lo, hi] as a view without copying — that is how you find “the smallest element not less than x”. In .NET Core 3.0+ the view and its Min are O(log n). But in Unity (and in .NET Framework) the view’s constructor immediately counts every element in the range — O(k), and for a range “from x to the maximum” that is up to O(n) per query.

The price: every node is an object on the managed heap, so every Add allocates, and the walk down causes cache misses. The set stores no duplicates: Add returns false, and elements with CompareTo == 0 count as the same. .NET has no multiset — you build one as a SortedDictionary<T, int> “value → how many times” or attach a unique id to each value.

SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> is the same tree over keys, O(log n). SortedList<TKey, TValue> is the opposite: two sorted arrays. Lookup is a binary search, O(log n), but inserting and removing in the middle is O(n), a shift. In return it is compact and offers access by position, Keys[i]. It suits data loaded once and then only read.
cards/7/deep:
Why the height is logarithmic. The red-black rules: a red node has no red children, and every path from the root to an empty leaf has the same number of black nodes. So the longest path (alternating black and red) is at most twice as long as the shortest (black only), hence height ≤ 2·log₂(n + 1). In the classic version an insert repairs the rules by recolouring and at most two rotations, a delete with at most three; SortedSet rebalances top-down, on the way to the insertion point, but the asymptotics are the same. An AVL tree is balanced more strictly: lookups are slightly faster, rotations more frequent.

The GetViewBetween view. A view is a window onto the same tree: changes to the set show up in it, and adding a value outside the range to the view throws. In .NET Core 3.0+ a view’s Min and Max are O(log n), while its Count is a walk over the range, O(k), repeated after every change to the set: do not call it in a loop. In .NET Framework and Unity (Mono) that walk is done by GetViewBetween itself, on every call. If you need a fast “nearest above” in Unity, search a sorted array yourself or write your own tree. If lo is greater than hi, you get an ArgumentException.

An empty set. Min and Max on an empty SortedSet do not throw; they return default(T): for int that is 0, which is easy to mistake for an answer.

The comparer decides what “equal” means. new SortedSet<Enemy>(Comparer<Enemy>.Create((a, b) => a.Hp.CompareTo(b.Hp))) silently refuses a second enemy with the same health. Hence the trick with an (Hp, Id) tuple: tuples compare field by field, left to right.
cards/8/q: A Unity project. Ability timers: every frame you need the one that fires next, and when a unit dies its timer is cancelled by id. Up to 10⁴ timers. What do you use?
cards/8/options/0: SortedSet<(float time, int id)> plus a dictionary id → time: Min, Add and Remove are O(log n), and Unity has all of it
cards/8/options/2: A List<(float time, int id)> sorted after every insert
cards/8/options/3: A Dictionary<int, float> id → time and a scan over all values to find the minimum
cards/8/explain: Three operations are needed: the minimum, an insert, and removing an arbitrary element. A red-black tree does all three in O(log n). The dictionary tells you the time a timer is stored with, so that you remove exactly the (time, id) tuple; the id in the tuple tells apart timers with the same time.
cards/8/wrong/1: Unity does not have it (.NET 6+). And in .NET, cancelling by id means either Remove from .NET 9 at O(n), or lazy deletion: mark cancelled timers and skip them when they come out.
cards/8/wrong/2: Sorting after every insert is O(n log n) per operation. Even inserting in the right place with BinarySearch and Insert is O(n) because of the shift.
cards/8/wrong/3: Insert and cancel are O(1), but finding the minimum scans every timer, O(n) every frame.
cards/9/title: LinkedList<T>, BitArray, and what .NET does not have
cards/9/body:
LinkedList<T> is a circular doubly linked list: every LinkedListNode<T> knows its neighbours, and inside the list the head’s previous node is the tail (from the outside, First.Previous still returns null). Inserting and removing by node — AddFirst, AddLast, AddAfter, Remove(node) — is O(1). But finding a node is a scan: Find and Remove(value) are O(n), and there is no index. Every node is a separate heap object: about 48 bytes per int versus 4 in an array, an allocation per insert and cache misses on traversal. The list pays off when the nodes are kept elsewhere, for example in a dictionary: that is how an LRU cache works.

BitArray is bits packed into an int[]: n/8 bytes versus n for a bool[]; Get and Set are O(1), and And, Or, Xor work on the whole array at once.

What the .NET standard library does not have: a deque — a double-ended queue, Deque<T> (replaced by LinkedList<T> at the cost of allocations, or by your own circular buffer); a multiset or a multimap; a direct “nearest above or below” on SortedSet — only via GetViewBetween; a trie and a disjoint-set union. In an interview you write these by hand — and that is fine.
cards/10/title: Unity: what .NET Standard 2.1 has and what it lacks
cards/10/body:
Unity 2021.2 and later compiles scripts as C# 9 against the .NET Standard 2.1 profile (or .NET Framework 4.x). Available: List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue, Stack, LinkedList, SortedSet, SortedDictionary, SortedList, BitArray, (int, int) tuples, HashCode, Span<T>, ArrayPool<T>, the dictionary’s TryAdd, TryDequeue and TryPop.

Missing is whatever came later: PriorityQueue (.NET 6), BitOperations (.NET Core 3.0; in Unity use math.countbits, math.lzcnt, math.tzcnt from Unity.Mathematics), CollectionsMarshal (.NET 5), Random.Shared and List<T>.EnsureCapacity (.NET 6). If you reach for PriorityQueue in a Unity interview, say that Unity lacks it and what you will use instead.

Jobs and Burst have their own collections from the com.unity.collections package: NativeArray, NativeList, NativeHashMap, NativeHashSet, NativeQueue. The memory lives outside the managed heap, elements must be unmanaged types, and you free it with Dispose(). More in the next lesson.
cards/11/q: Match the operation with its cost.
cards/11/pairs/3/1: O(log n): the new root sinks
cards/11/pairs/4/1: O(log n): a walk to the outermost node
cards/11/pairs/5/1: O(1): the node is already known
